title: Author's Preface to the Second Volume
paragraphs: The Americans live in a democratic social state, which has naturally led them to certain laws and a certain political character. This same social state has, moreover, produced among them a multitude of feelings and opinions that were unknown among the older aristocratic communities of Europe. It has destroyed or modified all the relationships that existed before and established new ones of a different kind. The face of civil society has been altered no less by these changes than that of the political world. I treated the first subject in the work on the Democracy of America that I published five years ago; to examine the second is the object of the present book. But these two parts complete each other and form one and the same work.

I must warn the reader at once against an error that would be extremely damaging to me. When he finds that I attribute so many different consequences to the principle of equality, he may conclude that I consider that principle the sole cause of everything taking place in the present age. But this would be to impute to me a very narrow view. A multitude of opinions, feelings, and tendencies now exist that owe their origin to circumstances unconnected with, or even contrary to, the principle of equality. If I were to take the United States as an example, I could easily show that the nature of the country, the origin of its inhabitants, the religion of its founders, their acquired knowledge, and their former habits have exerted, and still exert, a vast influence on the thoughts and feelings of that people, independently of democracy. Different causes, no less distinct from the circumstance of equality of conditions, could be traced in Europe, and would explain a great part of what is happening among us.

I acknowledge the existence of all these different causes, and their power, but my subject does not lead me to treat them. I have not undertaken to unfold the reason for all our inclinations and all our notions. My only aim is to show in what respects the principle of equality has modified both.

Some readers may perhaps be astonished that—firmly persuaded as I am that the democratic revolution we are witnessing is an irresistible fact against which it would be neither desirable nor wise to struggle—I have so often had occasion in this book to address language of such severity to the democratic communities that this revolution has brought into being. My answer is simply this: it is because I am not an enemy of democracy that I have tried to speak of democracy with complete sincerity.

Men will not accept truth from the hands of their enemies, and truth is seldom offered to them by their friends. For this reason I have spoken it. I was convinced that many would take it upon themselves to announce the new blessings the principle of equality promises humanity, but that few would dare to point out from afar the dangers with which it threatens them. I have therefore turned my chief attention to those perils, and believing I had seen them clearly, I did not have the cowardice to leave them untold.

I trust that my readers will find in this Second Part the same impartiality that seems to have been noted in the earlier work. Placed as I am in the midst of the conflicting opinions that divide us, I have tried to suppress within myself for a time the favorable sympathies or the adverse feelings with which each of them inspires me. If those who read this book can find a single sentence intended to flatter any of the great parties that have stirred my country, or any of the petty factions now harassing and weakening it, let such readers raise their voices to accuse me.

The subject I have tried to embrace is immense, for it includes the greater part of the feelings and opinions to which the new state of society has given birth. Such a subject is doubtless beyond my strength, and in treating it I have not succeeded in satisfying myself. But if I have not been able to reach the goal I had in view, my readers will at least do me the justice to acknowledge that I have conceived and pursued my undertaking in a spirit not unworthy of success.
Section I: Influence of Democracy on the Action of Intellect in the United States.
